unit.title: Use electrical software to draw simple circuits

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: Describe the steps you would follow to draw a simple lighting circuit in electrical drawing software, starting from a hand sketch.
essays.modelAnswer: I read the job brief and study the sketch, and I list the parts: the supply, the breaker or fuse, the switch, the lamps and the earth. I open the software and start a new drawing from the Centre's template, so the page size, border and title block are already set. I fill in the title block with the title, drawing number, date and my name. I turn on the grid and snap. Then I place the symbols from the software's standard library, arranged in a sensible order so the wires will not cross much. I connect them with straight wires that end exactly on each symbol's connection points, adding a junction dot only where wires join. I give each part its own label and add ratings such as '6 A'. I save the file often, with a clear name. Finally I check the drawing against the sketch, look at the print preview, print it and save a print-ready copy to send.
markingPoints: Reads the brief and sketch and lists the parts first
Starts from the template or sets up the page and fills in the title block
Places standard symbols from the library in a sensible order, using the grid
Joins wires correctly to connection points, with dots only at joins
Labels parts with ratings, saves often, checks against the sketch, prints or exports

essays.stem: Explain why standard symbols are used on circuit diagrams. Then describe four symbols and say what each one stands for.
essays.modelAnswer: Standard symbols are agreed shapes that mean the same thing to every electrician, designer and inspector, whoever drew the plan. This means a drawing can be read quickly and correctly without long notes, there is less chance of a mistake when the circuit is built, tested or repaired, and the drawing can be understood by people who speak different languages. Drawing software has these standard symbols ready-made, so they are drawn the same way every time. Four examples are: a lamp, shown as a circle with a cross inside it; a fuse, shown as a small rectangle with a line along its length; an earth, shown as a short upright line with three flat lines under it, each shorter than the one above; and a motor, shown as a circle with the letter M inside it. Others include a switch, drawn as a line with a gap and an angled arm, and a cell, drawn as one long and one short line.
markingPoints: Standard symbols mean the same to everyone who reads the drawing
They make drawings quick to read and reduce mistakes when building, testing or repairing
Software provides the standard symbols so they are drawn the same way each time
Two symbols described correctly
Two more symbols described correctly

essays.stem: Explain what information is put in the title block of a drawing, and why each item is needed.
essays.modelAnswer: The title block is a box, usually in the bottom right corner of the sheet, that gives the key facts about the drawing. The title says what the drawing shows, such as 'Room 4 lighting circuit'. The drawing number gives the drawing its own reference, so it can be filed and found again. The revision letter or number, with its date, shows which version this is, so that nobody works from an old copy. The names or initials of the person who drew it and the person who checked it show who is responsible for it. The date shows when it was made. The scale, or 'not to scale' for a circuit diagram, tells the reader whether measurements can be taken from it. The client or job name and the Centre or company name show who the drawing belongs to. The sheet number, such as '1 of 2', shows whether any pages are missing.
markingPoints: Title and drawing number, so the drawing is identified and can be found
Revision and its date, so the latest version is used
Drawn by and checked by, showing who is responsible
Date and scale (or 'not to scale')
Client or job name and the sheet number

essays.stem: Describe good habits for saving, naming and backing up drawing files, and say why each habit matters.
essays.modelAnswer: I save my work every few minutes and after every big change, so that a power cut or a computer fault does not lose much work. I give each file a clear name that tells what it is, with the job, the room, the revision and the date, for example 'Lighting-Room4_RevA'. A clear name makes the file easy to find and stops people opening the wrong version. I save files in the right job folder, not loose on the desktop. When I change a drawing that has already been issued, I use Save As to make a new revision, so the old one is kept for the record. I keep a backup copy on a second drive or on the Centre's online storage, so the work is safe if the computer fails or is stolen. I do not delete old revisions without permission, and I close files properly before shutting down the computer.
markingPoints: Saves often, so little work is lost after a power cut or fault
Clear file names with job, revision and date, so the right file is found
Files kept in the correct job folder
Save As for a new revision, keeping the old one
Backup copy on a second drive or online storage

essays.stem: Compare a circuit (schematic) diagram, a wiring diagram and a layout plan. Say what each one shows and when each is used.
essays.modelAnswer: A circuit diagram, or schematic, uses symbols to show how a circuit works: which parts are connected and the path the current takes. It does not show where the parts are, and the wires are drawn as straight lines so it is easy to follow. It is used to understand and design the circuit and to find faults. A wiring diagram, or connection diagram, shows how the parts are actually wired, terminal to terminal, often with wire numbers and the real positions of the terminals in the equipment. It is used when wiring a panel or a machine and when checking the connections. A layout plan is a drawing of the room or building, often to scale, showing where the lights, switches, sockets and the distribution board are placed, and sometimes the cable routes. It is used to mark out the job on site and to work out the materials needed.
markingPoints: Circuit diagram: shows how the circuit works with symbols, not where parts are
Use of the circuit diagram: design, understanding, fault-finding
Wiring diagram: terminal-to-terminal connections, used when wiring and checking
Layout plan: positions of lights, switches and sockets in the building, often to scale
Use of the layout plan: marking out on site and listing materials

essays.stem: Explain how you would check a finished drawing before you hand it in or issue it.
essays.modelAnswer: First I compare the drawing with the job brief and the sketch, part by part, to be sure nothing is missing and nothing extra has been added. I trace every wire from the supply through each part and back, to check that each connection is correct and that every wire end really joins a connection point. I check that junction dots are only where wires are meant to join. I check that each symbol is the right standard symbol, and that each part has its own label and a rating where needed, with no label used twice. I check the title block: title, drawing number, revision, date and my name. I check the spelling of all the text. If the software can check connections or simulate the circuit, I run that check. I look at the print preview to make sure everything fits and can be read. Then I ask another person to check it and sign the 'checked by' box.
markingPoints: Compares the drawing with the brief and the sketch
Traces every connection; dots only where wires join
Checks symbols, labels (none repeated) and ratings
Checks the title block and spelling
Uses the software check or simulation, print preview, and a second checker

essays.stem: Describe safe and healthy ways of working at a computer for long periods.
essays.modelAnswer: I sit on an adjustable chair with my back supported, my feet flat on the floor or on a footrest, and my knees at about a right angle. The top of the screen is at about eye level and about an arm's length away, so I do not bend my neck. The keyboard and mouse are close, so my wrists stay straight and my elbows stay by my sides. I set the screen brightness to suit the room and place the screen so there is no glare from windows or lights. I take a short break from the screen about every hour: I stand up, stretch, and look at something far away to rest my eyes. I keep food and drink away from the computer. I check that cables are tidy and are not a trip hazard, and that plugs and leads are not damaged. Any fault is reported, and that equipment is not used until it is repaired.
markingPoints: Good posture: adjustable chair, back supported, feet flat
Screen at about eye level and an arm's length away, no glare
Keyboard and mouse close, wrists straight
Regular short breaks and eye rest
Electrical and trip safety: no food or drink, tidy cables, damaged equipment reported

essays.stem: Explain how you would print a drawing, and save a copy to send by email, so that it is clear, complete and the right size.
essays.modelAnswer: Before printing I save the drawing. I open the page setup and choose the paper size and the page direction that match the drawing, usually landscape for circuit drawings. I choose the printer and check that it has paper and ink. I use print preview to make sure the whole drawing, the border and the title block are on the page and nothing is cut off. If the paper is smaller than the drawing, I choose 'fit to page' so it scales down, and I check that the text is still big enough to read. I print in black, or in colours that stay clear, with lines thick enough to see. I check the printout against the screen. To send it by email, I export it to a fixed, print-ready file such as a PDF, so the client can open and print it without the drawing software. I give it a clear file name with the revision, and I open it once to check it before sending.
markingPoints: Page setup: correct paper size and page direction
Print preview: whole drawing and title block on the page, nothing cut off
Fit to page if needed, text still readable, lines clear
Checks the printout against the screen
Exports a print-ready copy (such as PDF) with a clear name and checks it before sending

essays.stem: Explain how the drawing grid and the zoom tools help you draw a neat circuit in which every wire is properly joined.
essays.modelAnswer: The grid is a pattern of dots or lines on the screen at a set spacing. With snap turned on, the cursor jumps to the nearest grid point, so symbols and wire ends line up exactly. This means wire ends land on the symbols' connection points and the software treats them as joined, instead of leaving tiny gaps that look joined but are not. The grid also keeps wires straight and evenly spaced, so the drawing looks neat and is easy to read. Zooming in lets me see small details, such as whether a wire really reaches a connection point, or whether a junction dot is in the right place. Zooming out lets me see the whole drawing, check the layout and make sure everything fits inside the border. Zooming only changes the view on the screen; it does not change the size of the drawing.
markingPoints: The grid gives a set spacing, and snap makes items jump to grid points
Wire ends land on connection points, so they are really joined (no hidden gaps)
Wires stay straight and evenly spaced, so the drawing is neat
Zoom in to check details such as joins and dots
Zoom out to check the whole layout; zoom changes only the view

essays.stem: Explain how you would draw the control circuit for a motor that starts with a start push button and stops with a stop push button, and explain how the circuit works.
essays.modelAnswer: I draw two upright supply lines, with the control fuse at the top of the line side. Between them I draw one line for the coil circuit: from the fuse, through the overload contact, then the stop push button, then the start push button, then the contactor coil K1, to the other supply line. The stop button is a normally closed contact and the start button is a normally open contact. In parallel with the start button I draw a normally open auxiliary contact of the contactor, also labelled K1, as the hold-in contact. When the start button is pressed, the coil is energised and the contactor closes, which also closes the hold-in contact. When start is released, current keeps flowing through the hold-in contact, so the motor keeps running. Pressing stop, or the overload tripping, breaks the circuit, the coil drops out and the hold-in contact opens, so the motor stays off. I label every part and number each wire.
markingPoints: Correct series order: fuse, overload contact, stop, start, coil
Stop button normally closed; start button normally open
Hold-in contact of the contactor drawn in parallel with the start button, same label as the coil
Explains starting and holding in after start is released
Explains stopping by the stop button or the overload; parts labelled and wires numbered

practical1.title: Draw a one-way and a two-way lighting circuit with electrical software
practical1.brief: As a group, use the Centre's electrical drawing software to draw a lighting circuit for a classroom: one lamp controlled by a one-way switch, and two lamps controlled by two 2-way switches (stair-type switching), all fed from one breaker at the distribution board. The assessor gives the group a hand sketch and the job brief. Each member works at a computer and draws one part of the job: member 1 sets up the drawing (page, border and title block) and saves it to the group's job folder; members 2 and 3 draw the one-way and the two-way circuits; member 4 adds the labels, ratings and wire numbers; member 5 checks the drawing against the sketch and fills in the 'checked by' box (in a group of four, member 4 also does the check). Pass the file on in turn, so that every member places at least two symbols and draws at least two wires while the assessor watches. Save the drawing, print it, and export a print-ready copy. Photograph the screen at each stage below, and photograph the printout. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: A computer for each member, with the Centre's electrical drawing software
The job brief and a hand sketch of the lighting circuit
The Centre's drawing start file, with border and title block
The group's job folder on the Centre's drive or storage
A phone or camera to photograph the screen and the printout
photos: The screen showing the new drawing set up, with the title block filled in
The screen with all the symbols placed, before wiring
The screen showing the finished one-way circuit
The screen showing the finished two-way circuit, with the wires between the two switches
The screen zoomed in on a junction dot and a wire end on a connection point
The file saved in the job folder, with its name and revision showing
The printed drawing laid flat, with the title block readable
checklist: Set up the drawing correctly: page size, border and a complete title block
Used the correct standard symbol from the software for each part
Placed the symbols in a sensible order and drew straight, neat wires with square corners
Joined every wire end to a connection point, with dots only where wires join
Labelled every part and added ratings and wire numbers as the brief asks
Saved the file often, with a clear name and revision, in the job folder
Checked the drawing against the sketch and corrected any mistakes
Printed the drawing to fit the page and exported a print-ready copy
Sat correctly at the computer and took short breaks
safety: Keep food and drink away from the computers
Keep cables tidy and off the floor so that nobody trips
Do not use any computer, lead or plug that is damaged; report it to the instructor
Keep the screen at about eye level and take a short break about every hour
Follow the Centre's rules for computers and storage; do not install any software

practical2.title: Draw a motor starter's power circuit and start/stop control circuit with electrical software
practical2.brief: As a group, use the Centre's electrical drawing software to draw a direct-on-line (DOL) starter for a three-phase motor. On sheet 1, draw the power circuit: supply, isolator, fuses or circuit breaker, contactor main contacts, overload relay and motor. On sheet 2, draw the control circuit with a stop push button, a start push button, the contactor coil, the hold-in contact, the overload contact and a 'running' indicator lamp. The assessor gives the group the parts list. Share the work so that every member draws part of it while the assessor watches: for example, one member sets up both sheets and their title blocks, two members draw the power circuit, and two members draw the control circuit, with everyone labelling and numbering their own part. If the software can simulate, run a simulation: press start, release it, then press stop, and photograph the screen at each step. If it cannot, each member traces the circuit on screen for the assessor and explains what happens. Check the drawings together, then save and print both sheets. Photograph the screen at each stage below, and photograph the printouts.
materials: A computer for each member, with the Centre's electrical drawing software
The parts list for the DOL starter, from the assessor
The Centre's drawing start file, with border and title block
The group's job folder on the Centre's drive or storage
A phone or camera to photograph the screens and the printouts
photos: Both sheets set up, with title blocks filled in and sheet numbers (1 of 2, 2 of 2)
The finished power circuit on screen
The finished control circuit on screen, with the hold-in contact across the start button
The simulation, or a member tracing the circuit, with the motor running after start is released
The simulation, or a member tracing the circuit, after stop is pressed
The saved files in the job folder, with names and revisions showing
Both printed sheets laid side by side
checklist: Drew the power circuit in the correct order from the supply to the motor
Drew the stop button in series and the hold-in contact in parallel with the start button
Used the same label for the contactor coil and all its contacts (for example K1)
Used correct standard symbols and neat, straight wiring, with junction dots where needed
Numbered the wires and labelled every part with its rating
Ran the simulation, or traced the circuit, and explained how it starts, holds in and stops
Completed both title blocks with sheet numbers and saved with a clear name and revision
Printed both sheets so that they fit the page and can be read
safety: Keep food and drink away from the computers
Keep cables tidy and off the floor so that nobody trips
Do not use any computer, lead or plug that is damaged; report it to the instructor
Keep the screen at about eye level and take a short break about every hour
Follow the Centre's rules for computers and storage; do not install any software
